extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; practicing scientists and graduate students interested in philosophy and history of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing scientific theories, research practices, and scientific change (paradigms, normal science, revolutions). Focuses on what counts as legitimate problems, theory choice, and measures of progress in the sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzle-solving ability (dominant criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The demonstrated ability to set up and to solve puzzles presented by nature is, in case of value conflict, the dominant criterion for most members of a scientific group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes that scientists judge theories and research largely by their capacity to solve concrete puzzles; in crises puzzle-solving ability often decides theory choice. This criterion explains why communities prefer theories that produce effective problem solutions even when other values conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of prediction (particularly quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy of prediction, particularly of quantitative prediction, is one of the most useful criteria to distinguish earlier from more recent theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn lists quantitative predictive success as a key measure when comparing theories along a developmental line; it is a primary empirical criterion used by impartial observers to judge which theory is later/better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of different problems solved
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of different problems a theory solves is a central measure of its comparative worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theory that solves a greater variety of problems across its domain is judged superior; Kuhn groups this with predictive accuracy and subject-matter balance as useful distinguishing criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between esoteric and everyday subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance between esoteric (specialized) and everyday subject matter addressed by a theory is a criterion for evaluating its development and applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn suggests that the relative mix of subject matter a theory tackles helps distinguish its progress and scope; this is one of several practical values used to contrast theories historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, scope, and compatibility (secondary values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity, scope, and compatibility with other specialties are important but less decisive values in theory appraisal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn calls these 'less useful' than predictive accuracy or problem-solving count but acknowledges they remain determinants of scientific preference; they often play a role when other measures are comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigmatic fit / adherence to the community's paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should conform to the paradigm's answers to questions like what the fundamental entities are, how they interact, which questions are legitimate, and which techniques may be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science is 'a strenuous and devoted attempt to force nature into the conceptual boxes supplied by professional education'; research that fits the paradigm's conceptual framework is enabled and judged as legitimate by the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of problems and research agenda (community-defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific community defines which questions may legitimately be asked and what problems count as appropriate for research; legitimacy is a criterion for evaluating proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn stresses that effective research scarcely begins before the community accepts answers to foundational questions; proposals outside that set are often suppressed or treated as illegitimate until a paradigm shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomaly resolution and capacity to explain anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory's capacity to resolve persistent anomalies—observations that resist alignment with professional expectation—is a critical evaluative standard and a driver of revolutionary change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues that failure to assimilate anomalies can lead to crisis and to extraordinary investigations; the ability of a new theory to account for anomalous phenomena (and to re-evaluate prior facts) is a hallmark of its superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical fruitfulness / production of concrete research results
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete, reproducible research results produced under a viewpoint that can be described and shared are a crucial test of a view's fruitfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn notes that early concrete results verbalizable in shared vocabulary may persuade some practitioners even before full theoretical translation; growing numbers of such results signal a productive alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability / communicability between competing groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which research results and problem-statements can be translated and communicated between proponents of competing theories is an important practical criterion for comparison and persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation allows extended comparisons and the vicarious understanding necessary for persuasion; Kuhn emphasizes translation is difficult, often lengthy, and not always decisive, but essential for late-stage theory choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion/internalization (being 'native' to a paradigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond intellectual persuasion, genuine acceptance requires conversion—internalizing the new viewpoint so one 'goes native' in its language and problem-solving style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn distinguishes mere use of a theory as a foreigner from true internalization; effective contribution and evaluation within a paradigm often require that socialization and education produce native competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historiographic perspective: study original research activity rather than textbook accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating scientific claims or histories, prefer direct study of research activity and internal coherence within its time rather than relying on textbook presentations that are pedagogic and retrospective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn warns that textbooks present a persuasive, cumulative image that can obscure revolutions; historians and reviewers should examine original practices, problems, and the internal logic of past communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure progress by improved problem-solving rather than presumed ontological closeness to 'truth'
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific progress should be judged by later theories' superiority at solving puzzles, making quantitative predictions, and handling problems—not by an unobservable theory-independent match to what is 'really there'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn rejects the notion that successive theories necessarily approach an objective ontology; reviewers should therefore emphasize empirical and problem-solving gains when assessing claims of progress.
